metadata.title: Comparative evaluation of ChatGPT and Gemini in brain-computer interfaces patient education: A multi-dimensional analysis of reliability, accuracy, comprehensibility, and readability

abstract:
BACKGROUND
Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCI) are a type of life-altering neurotechnology, but their inherent complexity poses significant challenges to patient education. Large Language Models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT and Gemini, offer new possibilities to address this challenge. This study aims to conduct a multi-dimensional, rigorous comparative analysis of the performance of these two mainstream AI models in responding to common patient questions related to BCI.


METHODS
Through a structured process combining clinical expert consensus, literature review, and online patient community analysis, we identified 13 key patient questions covering the entire BCI treatment cycle. We then obtained responses to these questions from ChatGPT and Gemini on September 1, 2025. An evaluation panel, composed of clinical experts and non-medical professionals, conducted a blinded assessment of the response quality using standardized Likert scales across three dimensions: reliability, accuracy, and comprehensibility. Concurrently, we performed an objective, quantitative analysis of the response texts using the Flesch-Kincaid readability tests.


RESULTS
On core quality metrics such as reliability, accuracy, and comprehensibility, the performance of the two models was generally comparable, both demonstrating a high level of proficiency with only sporadic statistical differences on a few technical questions. However, a clear significant disparity emerged in the dimension of readability: for 12 of the 13 questions, the text generated by Gemini required a significantly lower reading grade level than that of ChatGPT (p < 0.05) and had significantly higher reading ease scores. This difference stemmed from Gemini's tendency to use shorter sentences and simpler vocabulary.


CONCLUSION
AI chatbots possess immense potential in the field of BCI patient education. Although both ChatGPT and Gemini can provide high-quality information, Gemini demonstrates a clear advantage in the accessibility and approachability of information, making it a potentially more suitable tool for initial application across diverse patient populations. Nevertheless, the limitations of AI in handling highly specialized and dynamically changing knowledge underscore the indispensable role of human expert supervision and validation in any clinical application.

Keywords Artificial intelligence  Brain-computer interface  Digital health  Health communication  Large language models  Patient education    1 Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), is reshaping the landscape of healthcare information dissemination [1 ,2 ]. This is particularly relevant as approximately half of the adult population consults the internet for health-related information before seeking professional medical advice [3 ]. LLMs, represented by OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini, have demonstrated immense potential in the field of patient education due to their ability to generate fluent, contextually relevant text [4–6 ]. These tools can translate complex medical concepts into easily understandable language, thus promising to bridge the information gap between healthcare professionals and patients, a value that has been preliminarily confirmed in studies across various fields such as oncology and diabetes management [7 ,8 ]. Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCI) are a form of advanced technology that integrates neuroscience, bioengineering, and clinical medicine. By establishing a direct communication pathway between the brain and external devices, it offers hope for the rehabilitation of patients who have lost function due to severe neurological injuries or degenerative diseases, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and spinal cord injury [9–11 ]. BCI systems are primarily divided into non-invasive and invasive categories, with the core difference being a trade-off between performance and risk. The performance of non-invasive BCIs is limited by the attenuation of neural signals as they pass through the skull, resulting in a relatively constrained signal-to-noise ratio and information transfer rate [12 ]. In contrast, invasive BCI, by implanting electrodes directly into the brain, can capture neural signals with extremely high spatiotemporal resolution that are less susceptible to interference [13 ]. However, the high technical complexity and surgical invasiveness upon which this superior performance relies present significant challenges for communication between clinicians and patients regarding risks, benefits, and expectations. Potential BCI recipients and their families must digest a vast amount of complex information about surgical risks, device calibration, neural plasticity, long-term maintenance, and the potential impact on personal identity and social life before making this critical decision [14 ]. Clear, accurate, and empathetic communication is the cornerstone of building physician-patient trust, ensuring the quality of informed consent, and managing patient expectations for treatment outcomes [15 ,16 ]. Research indicates that patients with a deep understanding of the etiology, pathophysiology, and treatment plan for their condition can more effectively participate in and adhere to treatment protocols, which directly contributes to better clinical outcomes [17 ]. However, the widespread variation in individual health literacy—the capacity to obtain, process, and understand basic health information to make appropriate decisions—poses a significant barrier to effective patient education. Recognizing this challenge, leading health organizations, including the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the American Medical Association, recommend that patient education materials be written at approximately a sixth-grade reading level to ensure comprehension across the broadest possible audience [18 ]. Adhering to this standard is crucial yet exceptionally difficult for a topic as complex as BCI. This further highlights the urgent market need for tools that can simplify technical information without sacrificing accuracy. Traditional brochures or limited clinic time are often insufficient to meet this need for deep, personalized information. In this context, LLMs appear to be a promising tool for addressing the challenges of BCI patient education. However, their effectiveness is not a given. Differences in the architecture, training data, and optimization objectives of various models can lead to significant variations in the quality and style of their responses [19–21 ]. Our study focuses specifically on OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini, as they are arguably the two most influential and widely adopted general-purpose LLMs currently available to the public. Their market leadership and high accessibility make them the most likely platforms patients would turn to for health information, establishing them as critical benchmarks for evaluating the utility of AI in patient education. A study by Elsenbawy et al. compared the performance of ChatGPT and Gemini in the field of general surgery, revealing the necessity of evaluating and comparing different AI models' utility in specific medical scenarios [22 ]. Currently, there is a lack of similar comparative research in the highly specialized field of BCI. Therefore, this study aims to fill this gap through a rigorous comparative analysis, thoroughly evaluating the performance of ChatGPT and Gemini in answering common patient questions related to BCI. Our research is not limited to assessing basic quality metrics such as reliability, accuracy, and comprehensibility; it also incorporates readability as a core evaluation dimension to investigate which model is better at generating accessible educational content suitable for the average patient's understanding. Through this analysis, we expect to provide empirical evidence and practical insights for integrating AI educational tools into BCI clinical practice.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study design This study was conducted as a comparative, cross-sectional analysis.  2.2 Question selection and construction To ensure the questions reflected genuine patient concerns, a research team composed of clinical experts in the field of neuromodulation first drew upon their extensive clinical experience to draft an initial list of questions most frequently asked by patients during brain-computer interface consultations. To validate and expand this list, we systematically reviewed existing brain-computer interface patient education materials, relevant medical literature, and, crucially, public patient support forums to capture authentic patient inquiries. Subsequently, we employed a modified two-round Delphi method to refine and prioritize this comprehensive list [23 ,24 ]. In the first round, members of the research team independently and anonymously rated each potential question on a 6-point Likert scale according to three criteria: frequency, based on clinical experience and forum analysis; importance, defined as its impact on patient decision-making; and complexity, representing the depth of information required for a satisfactory answer. After the results were aggregated, a ranked list was distributed for the second round. In this round, participants reviewed the team's anonymized scores and were given the opportunity to revise their own rankings, providing a brief justification if their score deviated significantly from the mean. This iterative process was designed to facilitate consensus in order to identify a set of questions that are not only frequently asked but are also deemed most critical for patient understanding and decision-making in real-world clinical scenarios. Ultimately, the 13 core questions that consistently received the highest aggregate scores were selected for this study. As shown in Table 1  , these questions were systematically categorized into three clinical time points: Pre-Implant, Implant, and Post-Implant.  2.3 Response generation and evaluation To ensure the rigor and reproducibility of the study, we adopted a standardized response generation protocol. On September 1, 2025, the research team input the 13 predetermined questions into the publicly available versions of ChatGPT (version 5.0, OpenAI) [25 ] and Gemini (version 2.5, Google) [26 ], respectively. Acknowledging that prior research has confirmed that minor variations in prompt wording can significantly affect the output of LLMs [27 ], we used a standardized prompt for all queries: “If you were a physician, how would you answer a patient asking …”. To account for output variability and ensure a comprehensive evaluation, we generated ten independent responses to each question from both models. Independence was ensured by initiating a new session for each query. Critically, the responses were not subjected to any form of screening or cherry-picking. The complete set of ten text outputs generated for each question was recorded in full and submitted to the evaluation panel, ensuring that our scoring process captured the typical and unfiltered performance of the models, rather than an idealized output. All generated responses were evaluated by a carefully assembled 10-person panel. The entire evaluation process strictly adhered to the principles of independence and blinding, meaning that evaluators were unaware of which AI model the response text originated from at the time of scoring. The composition of this panel was designed to balance professional and public perspectives: 8 members were senior clinical experts in the BCI field, primarily responsible for assessing the content's professionalism, accuracy, and reliability; the other 2 members were professionals with non-medical backgrounds but extensive experience in health communication or patient advocacy, who focused on evaluating the content's accessibility, clarity, and comprehensibility. This diverse evaluation structure ensured that our analysis could grasp both the scientific rigor of the content and its practical value as patient education material. The evaluation framework comprised two layers. The first was a subjective assessment of response quality using standardized Likert scales: Reliability (1–6 points), which assessed whether the information was consistent, coherent, from a credible source, and whether there was a risk of misleading statements or overpromising; Accuracy (1–3 points), which evaluated whether the information was fully consistent with current, recognized best practices and evidence in scientific and clinical fact; and Comprehensibility (1–3 points), which assessed whether the language was clear and concise, the logical structure was easy to follow, and unnecessary technical jargon was effectively avoided. The second layer was an objective quantitative analysis of readability. We employed the industry-recognized Flesch-Kincaid readability test suite to perform automated analysis on each response text [28 ], generating several objective metrics. The first metric, Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, maps text difficulty to the corresponding grade level in the U.S. education system, where a higher value indicates greater difficulty [29 ]. For instance, a score of 6.0 corresponds to a 6th-grade reading level, and therefore, any score above 6.0 is considered more difficult than the recommended level for patient materials [30 ]. The second metric is the Flesch Reading Ease Score, with a range of 0–100, where higher scores indicate the text is easier to read. Conversely, a lower score on this scale signifies greater difficulty. Scores in the 80–90 range are typically considered appropriate for a 6th-grade reading level, meaning scores below 80 represent a reading difficulty level higher than the 6th-grade benchmark. A score between 60–70 is generally considered “plain English” suitable for most adults. Finally, we analyzed micro-textual features, such as total word and sentence counts, average words per sentence, and average syllables per word. These features were used to deeply interpret the textual structure differences behind the grade level and ease scores.  2.4 Satistical analysis All Likert scale ratings collected from the evaluation panel and data from automated readability tests were presented as mean ± standard deviation (Mean ± SD). To assess the inter-rater reliability of the subjective scoring data, which included reliability, accuracy, and comprehensibility, we calculated the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC). This method was used to examine the degree of consistency among the 10-member evaluation panel when using the Likert scale for rating. The results indicated that the ICC values for all three subjective evaluation dimensions exceeded 0.75, demonstrating a high degree of agreement among the raters and thereby ensuring the reliability of the subjective scoring data. We used two-tailed, unpaired t-tests to compare the differences in means between ChatGPT and Gemini across all evaluation dimensions. All statistical calculations were completed using SPSS, Version 27.0 (IBM), with the threshold for statistical significance set at p < 0.05. This study did not involve any patients or access to patient-related data. Accordingly, it was formally exempted from review by the Institutional Review Board. All professionals serving on the evaluation panel were informed of the study’s purpose and methodology, and all voluntarily provided their consent to participate in the assessment process.   3 Results In the three fundamental dimensions of content quality—reliability, accuracy, and comprehensibility—both ChatGPT and Gemini performed at a very high level, demonstrating significant potential as reliable sources of information. The scores for both models showed no statistically significant differences on the vast majority of questions, indicating that their capabilities in generating factually accurate, logically clear, and easy-to-understand responses were comparable (Table 2  ). Despite the overall comparable performance, in the dimension of reliability, we observed statistically significant differences on two questions involving specific technical details, revealing subtle tendencies of the models in handling different types of information. For question Q6 (“How is the BCI device calibrated and programmed?”), a question concerning a specific technical process, Gemini's reliability score (5.6 ± 0.5) was significantly higher than ChatGPT's (4.8 ± 0.4, p  = 0.003). Conversely, for question Q11 (“What activities should be avoided with a BCI implant?”), a question related to lifestyle guidance and risk avoidance, ChatGPT's reliability score (5.5 ± 0.5) was significantly superior to Gemini's (5.0 ± 0.5, p  = 0.042). These findings suggest that although both models converge in their ability to explain macro-level concepts, they may have respective areas of strength in grasping micro-level, domain-specific knowledge details. In stark contrast to the parity in core quality metrics, a clear, substantial, and systematic gap existed between the two models in the dimension of readability (Table 3  ). For 12 of the 13 questions, the responses generated by Gemini required a significantly lower Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level than those from ChatGPT (p -values generally < 0.01). On average, the reading difficulty of Gemini's responses corresponded roughly to a lower-grade U.S. high school level, whereas ChatGPT's responses generally demanded a college-level reading ability. Highly correlated with this, Gemini's Flesch Reading Ease scores were also consistently and significantly higher, with most scores falling within or near the range considered “suitable for the general public,” while ChatGPT's scores were generally lower, indicating its text was less friendly to the average reader. To investigate the underlying reasons for this “readability gap,” we analyzed the micro-structural features of the text. The data revealed two distinctly different “communication strategies.” At the lexical and syntactic level, Gemini's responses, across multiple questions, had a significantly lower average number of syllables per word (p -values generally < 0.001), indicating a preference for more common, shorter words. Concurrently, its average number of words per sentence was also lower, resulting in a more concise sentence structure. At the content organization level, it was interesting to note that despite using simpler words and sentence structures, Gemini's responses contained significantly more sentences and a higher total word count for several questions. This suggests that Gemini employs a strategy of “breaking down the whole into parts and explaining patiently” to ensure informational completeness: it deconstructs complex concepts into more, shorter sentences, using a longer text to elaborate and explain, thereby effectively reducing the information density and cognitive load for the reader per unit of time.  4 Discussion The core contribution of this study is that it moves beyond a simple judgment of “right versus wrong” in AI-generated content to a deeper exploration of the complex dimension of “good versus bad” in information delivery. The findings reveal a phenomenon of critical importance for the application of LLMs in the medical field: even when performance on basic quality metrics like reliability and accuracy is comparable, different models can exhibit a significant variations in readability—the “last mile” that determines whether information can cross the “knowledge divide” and truly reach the patient. Our analysis clearly demonstrates that while both ChatGPT and Gemini can provide high-quality information to BCI patients, Google Gemini shows a systematic and decisive advantage in making this information accessible and digestible. In a frontier field like BCI, which has high technical barriers and is filled with unknowns and anxiety for patients, effective communication is about far more than conveying cold, accurate facts. Its core objective is empowerment—ensuring that patients can truly understand these facts and build their own cognitive framework upon them, thereby making autonomous medical decisions that align with their personal values [19 ,31 ]. Individual differences in health literacy are a significant barrier between medical information and patient understanding [32 ]. As highlighted by the research of Lo Bianco et al. in the field of SCS, the comprehensibility of patient education materials for complex neuromodulation technologies is a cornerstone for ensuring high-quality informed consent and building a strong physician-patient alliance [33 ]. Our study quantitatively validates this principle in the BCI field and forcefully argues that readability should not be considered a secondary, “nice-to-have” metric, but rather a core standard for evaluating the clinical utility of AI educational tools. A response that requires a college reading level on the Flesch-Kincaid test, no matter how precise its content, will have greatly diminished value for a patient with only a high school education, and may even have negative consequences due to misunderstanding [34 ]. Gemini, through its unique text generation strategy that favors simpler vocabulary and more concise syntax, effectively lowers the cognitive threshold for information. This theoretically makes it a more universally applicable tool, better able to serve a broad patient population with diverse educational backgrounds, cultural levels, and age structures. Although both models performed admirably on macro-level questions, the fluctuation in their reliability scores when dealing with specific technical details, such as device calibration and activity restrictions, serves as a warning. This highlights reveals the inherent challenges that current general-purpose LLMs face when handling highly specialized, rapidly evolving vertical domains. The fundamental reason is that the knowledge of these models is primarily derived from the vast but general internet corpora used during their training, which inevitably leads to limitations in their depth and precision in specific domains, as well as their ability to keep up with the latest clinical guidelines and technological advancements [35 ]. This finding is highly consistent with concerns in the literature about AI's potential for “hallucination” or its inability to escape “outdated information” [36 ,37 ]. This directly leads to a core principle that must be adhered to now and in the foreseeable future: any AI tool applied in a clinical setting must be strictly placed within a “human-in-the-loop” framework for supervision and validation. The role of AI should be that of an “intelligent assistant” or “efficiency multiplier” for clinicians, not an “autonomous decision-maker.” It can efficiently generate a well-structured and content-rich draft of educational material, but the final verification, revision, personalized supplementation, and, crucially, the delivery and interpretation tailored to the specific patient's clinical condition, psychological state, and individual needs must be performed by medical professionals equipped with expert knowledge and human empathy [31 ,34 ]. AI can optimize the “content” of communication, but it cannot replace the “process” of communication [38 ]. The significant differences in communication strategies observed between ChatGPT and Gemini may reflect different philosophies of their respective development teams regarding model training and optimization objectives. Perhaps Gemini was designed with a greater emphasis on simulating fluent, natural, everyday conversation, thus predisposing it to generate text that is easily understood by the general public. In contrast, ChatGPT's training may have focused more on knowledge depth and logical rigor, leading to a linguistic style that is more formal and academic [39 ,40 ]. This principle is especially critical given that patients increasingly turn to a wide array of online sources for health information, with platforms like YouTube and other web channels being among the most popular [41 ]. The variable quality and reliability of information on such platforms underscore the urgent need for rigorously validated tools like the LLMs we evaluated, which, when properly supervised, can provide a more dependable source of patient education [42 ]. This speculation raises a broader consideration: when developing or selecting AI tools for the healthcare sector, we may need to move beyond the simple question of “which model is better” and instead consider “which model is more suitable for which specific task.” There is no “one-size-fits-all” AI. A model that excels at helping a doctor draft an academic paper may not be the best choice for explaining surgical risks to a patient. The future direction may lie in developing and training highly specialized LLMs targeted at specific medical scenarios and communication goals. 4.1 Limitations This study presents a direct, multidimensional comparison of leading large language models for patient education on brain-computer interfaces. We ensured professional rigor through clinically-developed questions and a blind evaluation by a multidisciplinary expert team. Significantly, our assessment moved beyond traditional accuracy to integrate reliability, comprehensibility, and in-depth readability analysis, providing a more comprehensive and clinically-oriented framework for valuing AI tools in medicine. Despite these methodological strengths, the conclusions of this study should be interpreted with caution, as it has several inherent limitations that also point the way for future research. The primary limitation of this study is the lack of direct patient involvement; we only simulated a public perspective through professionals. This highlights the necessity of conducting patient-centered, prospective clinical validation in the future to directly measure the actual impact of AI-assisted education on patient knowledge levels, decisional conflict, and anxiety. Furthermore, this study is essentially a static, cross-sectional evaluation of specific LLM versions and fails to capture the rapid iteration of technology and the inherent deficiencies of general models in handling highly specialized knowledge. Additionally, our readability analysis relied on a single online calculator for the Flesch-Kincaid tests. As the use of a single tool can sometimes yield variability in results, future studies could enhance robustness by averaging scores from multiple validated calculators [43 ]. Therefore, future research should shift towards the fine-tuning and development of domain-specific models, exploring the use of high-quality, specialized BCI literature to train models to enhance their accuracy and reliability. Lastly, although the 13 questions selected for this study are representative, they do not cover all patient concerns, nor do they explore how to seamlessly integrate AI tools into complex clinical workflows. This requires future work to focus on the construction and evaluation of human-AI collaborative clinical workflows by developing and validating standardized integration pathways to pave the way for this technology to move from theory to safe and effective clinical practice.   5 Conclusion Through a rigorous comparative analysis of ChatGPT and Gemini, this study confirms that LLMs hold immense, yet largely untapped, potential for providing educational support to BCI patients. The core finding is that although both models perform comparably in terms of information reliability and accuracy, there is a significant difference in the crucial dimension of readability. Gemini, with its systematic advantage in generating more accessible text, shows that it may have broader clinical applicability as a preliminary information communication tool for patients with varying levels of health literacy. However, we must emphasize that AI tools still have inherent limitations when dealing with highly specialized and dynamically updated knowledge. Therefore, in any clinical application scenario, AI should be positioned as a supplement and enhancement to the traditional physician-patient communication model, not a replacement. The supervision, validation, and personalized interpretation by human experts play an indispensable “gatekeeper” role in ensuring medical quality and patient safety. Ultimately, leveraging the power of AI responsibly means seamlessly integrating it into a human-centered, clinician-led communication framework to truly empower BCI patients, making them more informed and confident participants in this life-changing medical journey. key_findings.claim: ChatGPT 5.0 and Gemini 2.5 performed comparably on reliability, accuracy, and comprehensibility for BCI patient education questions, with statistically significant differences on only 2 of 13 questions for reliability and no significant differences on accuracy or comprehensibility for any question.
key_findings.quantitative_result: No significant differences on 11/13 questions for reliability; no significant differences on all 13 questions for accuracy and comprehensibility (all p > 0.05 except Q6 and Q11 reliability)
key_findings.context: 10-person blinded evaluation panel using Likert scales; ICC > 0.75 for all dimensions confirming inter-rater reliability

key_findings.claim: Gemini 2.5 generated text with significantly lower Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level than ChatGPT 5.0 for 12 of 13 BCI patient questions, indicating substantially better readability for general audiences.
key_findings.quantitative_result: 12/13 questions p < 0.05; ChatGPT responses generally at college reading level, Gemini at lower high school level
key_findings.context: Automated Flesch-Kincaid analysis on 10 independent responses per question per model

key_findings.claim: Gemini 2.5 achieved significantly higher Flesch Reading Ease scores than ChatGPT 5.0 for 12 of 13 questions, with most Gemini scores approaching the range considered suitable for general public comprehension.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Example Q10: Gemini ease score 60.3 ± 4.8 vs ChatGPT 44.9 ± 7.7 (p < 0.001); Q1: Gemini 40.3 ± 3.7 vs ChatGPT 23.0 ± 6.1 (p < 0.001)
key_findings.context: Flesch Reading Ease scale 0–100; scores 60–70 considered plain English for most adults; scores 80–90 appropriate for 6th-grade level

key_findings.claim: Gemini's readability advantage over ChatGPT is driven by lower average syllables per word and, in some questions, shorter sentences, while Gemini also produced more total sentences and higher word counts, suggesting a 'decomposition' communication strategy.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Syllables/word significantly lower for Gemini on most questions (p < 0.001 for many); Gemini produced more sentences for Q6 (10.3 ± 0.7 vs 8.8 ± 0.8, p = 0.001), Q10 (10.0 ± 0.8 vs 7.8 ± 0.6, p < 0.001), Q11, Q12
key_findings.context: Micro-textual feature analysis across 13 questions with 10 responses each

key_findings.claim: Gemini demonstrated significantly higher reliability than ChatGPT for the technically specific question about BCI device calibration and programming (Q6).
key_findings.context: Question: 'How is the BCI device calibrated and programmed?'

key_findings.claim: ChatGPT demonstrated significantly higher reliability than Gemini for the lifestyle guidance question about activities to avoid with a BCI implant (Q11).
key_findings.context: Question: 'What activities should I avoid with a BCI implant?'

key_findings.claim: Neither ChatGPT 5.0 nor Gemini 2.5 responses met the recommended 6th-grade reading level standard for patient education materials, with ChatGPT performing worse; mean grade levels ranged approximately 11–16 for ChatGPT and 9–14 for Gemini.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Grade levels across questions: ChatGPT 11.8–16.1, Gemini 8.6–13.9; recommended level is grade 6 (Flesch-Kincaid Grade ≤ 6)
key_findings.context: US Department of Health and Human Services and American Medical Association recommend 6th-grade reading level for patient materials

key_findings.claim: Both LLMs show inherent limitations in handling highly specialized, rapidly evolving BCI knowledge, underscoring the necessity of human-in-the-loop supervision for clinical deployment.
key_findings.context: Inferred from reliability score fluctuations on technical questions and discussion of AI hallucination risks

llm_extraction.methods_summary: Cross-sectional comparative study evaluating ChatGPT 5.0 and Gemini 2.5 on 13 BCI patient education questions. Questions were selected via a modified two-round Delphi method combining clinical expert consensus, literature review, and online patient forum analysis. On September 1, 2025, 10 independent responses were generated per question per model using a standardized physician-role prompt, with each response generated in a new session to ensure independence. A 10-person blinded evaluation panel (8 BCI clinical experts, 2 health communication professionals) rated responses using Likert scales for reliability (1–6), accuracy (1–3), and comprehensibility (1–3). Inter-rater reliability was assessed via intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC > 0.75 for all dimensions). Objective readability analysis used the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, Flesch Reading Ease Score, average words per sentence, average syllables per word, sentence count, and word count. Statistical comparisons used two-tailed unpaired t-tests with significance threshold p < 0.05; analysis performed in SPSS v27.0.
llm_extraction.limitations: Primary limitation is absence of actual patient participants; public perspective was simulated through non-medical professionals rather than direct patient-centered validation. The study is a static cross-sectional snapshot of specific LLM versions (ChatGPT 5.0, Gemini 2.5) that does not capture rapid model iteration. Readability analysis relied on a single online Flesch-Kincaid calculator, introducing potential measurement variability. The 13 questions, while representative, do not comprehensively cover all BCI patient concerns. The study does not evaluate how AI tools integrate into real clinical workflows. The evaluation panel is small (n=10) and no sample size justification was provided. No direct patient outcome measures (knowledge retention, decisional conflict, anxiety) were assessed.

relationships.description: Extends Elsenbawy et al.'s comparison of ChatGPT and Gemini in general surgery patient education to the specialized domain of brain-computer interfaces, using a more rigorous multidimensional framework that adds readability as a core metric.

Extends Lo Bianco et al.'s evaluation of AI responses for spinal cord stimulation (SCS) patient questions by applying a similar reliability/accuracy/comprehensibility framework to BCI and adding quantitative readability analysis.

Supports Nasra et al.'s systematic review finding that AI can improve patient education material readability, specifically demonstrating that Gemini generates more accessible text than ChatGPT for a specialized neuromodulation topic.

Corroborates Kara et al.'s findings comparing ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity on ankylosing spondylitis questions, reinforcing the pattern of Gemini generating more readable text than ChatGPT in medical patient education contexts.

Aligns with Zhou et al.'s comparative analysis of AI-generated patient education for spinal surgeries, confirming that readability differences between LLMs are a consistent and clinically meaningful finding across medical specialties.

methodology_details.approach: Cross-sectional blinded comparative evaluation of two LLMs (ChatGPT 5.0, Gemini 2.5) using expert panel Likert-scale scoring and automated Flesch-Kincaid readability analysis on 13 BCI patient education questions with 10 responses each
